title: Systems Analyst: what the system must do, and proof that it does
intro: An analyst bridges the business and the builders: gathers requirements, models data and process, sizes the system, checks feasibility, and traces every requirement to a test.
outcome: A testable requirements list traced to tests, a data dictionary and ER diagram, sizing numbers, a cost-benefit case and a feasibility verdict.

steps.title: Write the problem statement and list stakeholders
steps.what: Everything is judged against the problem.
how: One paragraph: who has what problem, and what it costs.
List stakeholders and what each cares about; use the Source field on requirements for this.
steps.done_when: A reader could tell if a proposal solves the problem.
mistakes: Writing the solution instead of the problem.
steps.ask: Help me write a problem statement.

steps.title: Capture requirements
steps.what: Each requirement is one testable statement.
how: Open Requirements and add each as 'The system shall...'.
Mark type (functional, non-functional, constraint) and priority (MoSCoW).
Write an acceptance criterion someone could check.

steps.title: Model the data
steps.what: The dictionary says what every field means.
how: Open Data dictionary: tables, columns, keys, null % and distinct counts.
Check relationships and orphans.
Copy the Mermaid diagram into mermaid.live.
steps.done_when: Every table has a description and orphans are 0.
steps.ask: Describe each table in my data dictionary.

steps.title: Model the process
how: Open Process analysis: duration percentiles, variability, bottleneck.
High variability (CV above 1) means unpredictable delivery.
mistakes: Optimising a step that isn't the bottleneck.
steps.ask: Where is my process bottleneck and why?

steps.title: Size the system
how: Queueing: enter arrival and service rates; keep utilisation under about 80%.
Availability: set an SLO; read error budget; combine components serial or parallel.
Capacity: enter load, capacity, growth; read months to full.
steps.done_when: You have a number for staffing, uptime and capacity.
steps.ask: How many servers or staff do I need?

steps.title: Make the cost-benefit case
how: Enter upfront cost, annual benefit and cost, years, discount rate.
Read NPV, ROI, IRR, payback.
Test with a lower benefit.
steps.done_when: NPV is positive even with pessimistic benefit.

steps.title: Score feasibility (TELOS)
how: Score each 1 to 5 with a note of evidence.
A single score below 3 caps the verdict.
steps.done_when: A verdict and a named weakest area.

steps.title: Trace requirements to tests
steps.what: Proof the system does what was agreed.
how: Set status as items are built then tested.
Fill the test reference.
Read the gaps list until empty.
steps.done_when: 80%+ of built requirements have a test.

steps.title: Audit how systems connect and which numbers matter
steps.what: Many businesses hold the same information in several systems and rely on people to copy it between them. A single source of truth means each piece of information has one owner system and the others copy from it. First map the systems and the manual hand-offs, then check that the metrics you report support real decisions.
how: Open Systems analysis > Single source of truth > Systems connectivity, load the sample and read the manual transfers and the information with no master.
List five systems from a business you know, mark the master for each kind of information with *, and say how each one sends data on.
Open Metric audit, load the sample and read why three of five metrics need work.
Start from three decisions the business makes, then list the metrics and reports that serve each, and cut the rest.
Pick the highest-priority manual transfer and write what it would take to automate it.
steps.done_when: You can explain why connecting systems is not the same as a single source of truth, and name a decision, an owner and a review habit for each metric you keep.
mistakes: Declaring a system 'connected' when people still re-key the data.
Choosing metrics first and decisions afterwards.
Letting two reports show the same metric with different definitions.
steps.ask: We keep customer details in the CRM, the ERP and a quotes spreadsheet. Which should be the master and how do I get there?

steps.title: Audit your documents and key-person risk
steps.what: Documents and know-how often live in shared drives and in one person's head. Structure them (one location, one owner, one current version) and ask the succession question: if this person left tomorrow, what would happen at the next audit?
how: Open Document inventory, load the sample and read the duplicates, version words in titles and missing owners.
List ten critical documents from a real or invented business and run them through the check.
Open Search time cost and estimate what looking for information costs a year; then plan a timed test to replace the guesses.
Open Key-person risk, load the sample and read who is exposed and which deadlines are close.
Write a succession plan for the most concentrated person: backups, written procedures and a practice run.
steps.done_when: You can say what makes a document trustworthy (owner, location, one current version, review date) and answer the 'if they left tomorrow' question for any role.
mistakes: Putting the version in the file name (final_v2_new).
Naming a backup who has never done the task.
Quoting a time-wasted figure you did not measure.
steps.ask: Our quality manager holds every audit procedure in her head. How do I reduce that risk in 90 days?
